item.title: Playground
item.description:
Open the playground →

The playground is go-slides itself, v0.13.0, compiled to WebAssembly and running in your browser. Type a deck on the left; the slides follow on the right. Nothing is sent to a server: not the deck, not a share link.

What it has

  • Live preview of every slide, rendered off the page’s thread (a Web Worker), so typing never waits for it. Click a slide to move the editor to its line; move the caret and the preview scrolls to its slide.

  • Slideshow: the presentation itself, with the keyboard, the on-screen controller and the transitions.

  • Presenter view: Present (or p in the slideshow) opens it in a second window: the current slide, the next step, the speaker notes (the deck’s <!-- comments -->), a clock and a timer. The arrow keys, Space, Home and End work in either window, and each follows the other, also when you edit the deck. If the window does not open, allow pop-ups for the site. The overview view (o) is in the downloaded page only.

  • Completion as you type: directive keys (spot _ ones in comments), the values of kind, theme, size, paginate, and template functions and data fields inside {{ }}.

  • Help for what is under the caret: a directive, a kind (what it sets), a template function. The help pane also links to these pages.

  • Problems on their line: template, YAML and HCL errors are highlighted in the editor and listed under it, and the preview keeps the last deck that rendered.

  • Examples: a welcome deck, templates that generate slides, slide kinds, an HCL front matter, themes and spot directives, and math, images and backgrounds (![bg], a split ![bg left:40%], filters).

  • Files: the panel left of the editor is the deck’s project, laid out the way the command and the VS Code extension read it: deck.md, slides.yaml, themes/, kinds/, media/.

    • Click a file to edit it. The editor colours it by its language (Markdown, YAML, HCL, JSON, CSS) and marks its problems.
    • Right-click (or Shift+F10) for New File, New Folder, Rename (F2), Delete (asks first) and New theme / New kind. Drag a file onto a folder to move it. The keyboard follows the WAI-ARIA tree pattern, type-ahead included.
    • Project ▸ New theme makes themes/my-gaia.css (or from default, uncover): @import of the built-in theme and the rules you add. It joins the Theme list. New kind and New data file start from templates too. Each is listed in slides.yaml, so slides build deck.md finds it.
    • Project ▸ Download project (.zip) saves it all. Unzipped, slides build deck.md builds it. Open project takes a .zip or a folder back. An archive that leaves its folder (.., absolute paths), holds more than 256 files or 8 MiB in a file, or inflates more than 100 times is refused.
    • Everything is kept in this browser with the draft. A project holds up to 64 MiB, and the line under the files says how much is used.

  • Media: drop or paste an image, a video or a sound on the editor and it goes into media/, and the deck names it: ![](media/photo.png). Drop files on a folder of the panel to put them there. The deck stays small and readable, and nothing is uploaded. The preview’s sandbox loads them without being opened up (the page hands it the bytes). Save as ▸ HTML page puts them in the page. https: images work too, but the browser fetches them from their server, which then sees your address. The preview sends no referrer.

  • Resizable panes: the file panel, the editor, the slide thumbnails, the preview and the help are separated by bars you can drag (the pointer becomes a resize cursor over one). The pane beside the bar takes the room, the others keep their size. Double-click a bar, or press Enter on it, to pull the pane shut and bring it back. From the keyboard, F6 moves between the bars, the arrow keys move one by 16 px, Home and End take the pane before it to its smallest and largest, and Escape returns to the editor. The View tab still switches panes off. The sizes you set are kept in this browser, with the draft; the default sizes (190, 168 and 280 px, the editor and the preview sharing the rest 6 to 5) are never stored.

  • Format: the Format tab edits the Markdown for you, and each press is one step of Undo.

    • Text: Bold, Italic, Strikethrough and Inline code work on the selection or the word at the caret and toggle (Ctrl+B, Ctrl+I, Ctrl+Shift+X and Ctrl+E; Cmd on a Mac). A button shows pressed when the caret is inside its marks. Markdown has no underline: Underline (Ctrl+U) wraps the text in <u>…</u>, a tag Marp’s default HTML allow-list keeps, so it works with raw HTML off.
    • Paragraph: Heading 1 to 3 (Ctrl+Alt+1..3), bullets (Ctrl+Shift+8), numbering (Ctrl+Shift+7) and a quote work on the selected lines and toggle. The horizontal rule is the <hr> tag: ---, *** and ___ would each start a new slide in Marp.
    • Table: a grid picks the columns and rows. At the caret in a table you add or remove a row or a column and align the column (:--, :-:, --:); the table is rewritten aligned after each edit.
    • Slide text left, centre or right writes a <style scoped> block into the current slide. Marp has no alignment syntax, and a style attribute does not pass the default HTML allow-list, but the scoped block does, so it works with raw HTML off and shows in the preview, the HTML page and the PDF.
    • Link (Ctrl+K) writes [text](url) with the url selected.

  • Highlighting of the front matter’s keys at any depth, in YAML (also in {a: 1} mappings) and in HCL.

  • Theme picker: default, gaia, uncover, the project’s themes (themes/*.css) and the themes the deck defines (/* @theme name */ in a <style>). It writes theme: into the front matter, YAML or HCL, so a shared link keeps it, and it follows the front matter when you edit it.

  • The preview keeps its place as you type: only the slides that changed are replaced, and a change of theme reopens the preview on the same slide.

  • Share link: the deck travels in the link itself (in its # part, compressed), so opening the link opens the deck. Links carry up to 64 KiB compressed, and the deck only: when the project holds more (themes, kinds, media), Share says so and offers the .zip.

  • Save as:

    • the HTML page, the same as slides deck.md writes;
    • a PDF (vector, its text selectable, with the outline);
    • an editable PowerPoint or OpenDocument deck.

    They are made in your browser, by the same code as slides --pdf, --pptx and --odp: the 100-slide benchmark deck’s PDF is byte-identical to the command’s. The first export downloads the export engine (about 5 MiB, once; your browser keeps it until the next update), with a progress line, and compiles it as it arrives. Then it downloads only the fonts your slides draw. On a 3 MB/s link the first PDF of the welcome deck is ready in under 3 seconds. The 100-slide deck then takes about 3 seconds. An https: image is included only if its server allows it (CORS); data: images always are.

  • Your draft is kept:

    • The deck is saved in this browser as you type (IndexedDB, for this site only) and comes back when you reload. Nothing is sent anywhere. The project’s text files (themes, kinds, data, slides.yaml) are kept the same way, even when you close the tab right after typing; media are stored as they are dropped.
    • A shared link opens its deck and keeps your draft: Draft ▸ Restore my draft brings it back.
    • An example, Draft ▸ Reset to the example (which asks first) and another tab never erase it either: Draft ▸ Restore replaced swaps it back.
    • Draft ▸ Forget my drafts erases everything stored.

Every export renders the project the preview shows: its slides.yaml, themes, kinds, data files and media, the media inside the document.

Images as files (slides --images) are not made in the browser: use the command or the VS Code extension.

Security

The deck is shown in an iframe sandboxed without the page’s origin: it can reach neither the playground nor its storage, submit no form and navigate nothing. Its page carries a Content Security Policy that runs only its own scripts. Raw HTML in the deck follows Marp’s allowlist, as slides does by default. A render that runs for more than 5 seconds (a template that loops) is stopped.

The presenter window keeps that sandbox. It is opened by the playground itself and shows the deck in an iframe sandboxed the same way. The two iframes cannot share storage, so the playground relays the slide number between them in messages. No frame that runs the deck gets the playground’s origin.

The project’s media reach the sandboxed frames as bytes in a message, and each frame makes its own blob: URLs of them, in its own origin. A blob: URL made by the playground does not load there, and the frames’ policy gains only blob: for media and fonts.

The playground can be served from your own machine, behind a sign-in: see Self-hosting.

Size and speed

The module is 8.8 MiB as GitHub Pages serves it (gzip; Pages does not serve brotli). It is downloaded once with a progress bar, then cached by the browser until the next deploy. On an Apple M4 Max with Chrome 155, measured against the live page, the editor is ready 2.1 s after the page opens, 1.5 s of which is the download, and the first slides appear at 2.4 s. A change to the 100-slide benchmark deck reaches the preview in about 30 ms: go-slides renders only the slides that changed, and only those are replaced in the preview.

item.title: Self-hosting
item.description:
The playground is static files, and slides --server is one process on the loopback. Both can run on your own machine, behind your own name, for people who sign in with your organisation’s account. This page does it with Caddy (tested with v2.11.7), which obtains and renews the HTTPS certificates itself, and oauth2-proxy for the sign-in. Every file shown here is in selfhost/, and its CI checks each Caddyfile with caddy validate.

The playground

Each release of the site attaches the whole site, playground included, as one tarball built for the root of a domain, with its SHA-256:

curl -fLO https://github.com/go-slides/go-slides.github.io/releases/download/v0.1.0/go-slides-site-v0.1.0.tar.gz
curl -fLO https://github.com/go-slides/go-slides.github.io/releases/download/v0.1.0/go-slides-site-v0.1.0.tar.gz.sha256
sha256sum -c go-slides-site-v0.1.0.tar.gz.sha256
tar -xzf go-slides-site-v0.1.0.tar.gz -C /srv
mv /srv/go-slides-site-v0.1.0 /srv/go-slides-site

The tarball is reproducible: building the same tag again gives the same bytes. Beside every file that compresses (the WebAssembly modules, the fonts, the pages, the scripts) it carries the same file compressed with Brotli (.br) and gzip (.gz), so the server sends them as they are and compresses nothing on the fly.

Caddyfile

slides.example.org is your name. Its A and AAAA records point at the machine, and ports 80 and 443 reach Caddy:

import headers.caddy

slides.example.org {
 root * /srv/go-slides-site
 file_server {
 precompressed br gzip
 }
 import playground_headers
}
caddy run --config Caddyfile.playground

The playground is then at https://slides.example.org/playground/.

What the server must get right

  • HTTPS. Caddy gets the certificate from Let’s Encrypt with ACME (RFC 8555), proving that it holds the name by answering on port 80 (HTTP-01) or 443 (TLS-ALPN-01), and renews it. A machine that the CA cannot reach can use the DNS-01 challenge instead (a TXT record, which needs a Caddy built with your DNS provider’s module), or your own certificate with tls cert.pem key.pem. On a test machine, tls internal uses Caddy’s local CA.
  • application/wasm. Caddy sends this type for .wasm; another server may need to be told. The playground compiles its modules from the bytes it has read (the export engine as it downloads, in a response of its own with that type), so it starts even from a server that sends another type; with nosniff, the right type is still the one to send.
  • Compression. precompressed br gzip sends playground.wasm.br to a browser that accepts Brotli, .gz to one that accepts gzip, and the file itself otherwise, with Vary: Accept-Encoding. The editor’s module is about 7 MiB in Brotli, against 33 MiB uncompressed.
  • Caching. The page asks for every module, worker, font and picture with the release in the query (playground.wasm?v=v0.1.0), so those can be kept for a year (immutable). The pages themselves are revalidated (no-cache): a new release is seen at the next visit.
  • The headers in headers.caddy:
(playground_headers) {
 header {
 Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'; worker-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https:; img-src 'self' data: blob: https:; media-src 'self' data: blob: https:; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https:; font-src 'self' data: blob: https:; frame-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'"
 X-Content-Type-Options nosniff
 Referrer-Policy no-referrer
 Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000"
 }
 @versioned query v=*
 header @versioned Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"
 @unversioned not query v=*
 header @unversioned Cache-Control "no-cache"
}

The policy is the one the playground needs: its scripts (the loader is inline), its WebAssembly ('wasm-unsafe-eval') and its worker, all from your server. A deck’s pictures, style sheets and fonts may come from any https: address, as they do in the command’s output; drop https: from img-src, style-src, font-src, media-src and connect-src to keep every request on your server, and decks that point elsewhere show without those resources. The deck itself runs in iframes sandboxed without your origin, under a stricter policy of their own that the playground writes into each frame: it cannot reach the playground, its storage or your cookies, whatever this header says. frame-ancestors 'self' stops other sites from framing the playground.

  • No COOP or COEP. The playground uses neither SharedArrayBuffer nor threads, so it does not need to be cross-origin isolated. Sending Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp would block a deck’s pictures from other sites.

Without the network

Once the page is loaded, everything happens in the browser: the editor, the preview, the presenter view, and the PDF, PPTX and ODP exports, whose fonts are in the tarball. The deck is sent neither to your server nor anywhere else. What needs the network is what the deck names: pictures or style sheets at an https: address, and the gaia theme’s web font, which it asks of fonts.bunny.net (without it, the slides fall back to another font). The links to this documentation leave your server.

slides --server behind the proxy

slides --server stays on 127.0.0.1 and Caddy forwards to it. The server checks the Host header of each request and the Origin of each live reload’s WebSocket, against DNS rebinding and other sites’ pages, and the proxy keeps the public name in both. --allowed-host adds that name to what the checks accept; they stay on:

slides -s --allowed-host decks.example.org /srv/decks
decks.example.org {
 reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080
}

The live reload goes through as it is (Caddy proxies WebSockets without configuration). Do not use --host 0.0.0.0 for this: it serves the directory to the whole network, around the proxy and its sign-in.

--allowed-host comes after v0.13.0. Until the next release, install the commit that has it: go install github.com/go-slides/slides/cmd/slides@v0.13.1-0.20261026090714-2e1da79f663e.

Sign-in with OpenID Connect

Caddy asks oauth2-proxy about every request (forward_auth). oauth2-proxy answers 202 for a browser that has signed in, which Caddy then serves, and 401 otherwise, which Caddy turns into a redirect to the sign-in. The sign-in is the authorization code flow of OpenID Connect Core 1.0: the browser goes to your provider (Keycloak, Authentik, Entra ID, Google, Okta, Dex…), comes back to /oauth2/callback with a code, oauth2-proxy exchanges the code for an ID Token, checks it, and sets its own cookie.

  1. Register a client with your provider, confidential, with the authorization code flow. Its redirect URIs, which must match exactly: https://slides.example.org/oauth2/callback and https://decks.example.org/oauth2/callback.
  2. Put the secrets in files readable by oauth2-proxy alone: the client’s secret, with no newline at the end, and a cookie secret of exactly 32 random bytes (head -c 32 /dev/urandom). Your secret store writes them (systemd credentials, Docker or Kubernetes secrets, Vault…); neither goes into a configuration file, a command line or an environment variable, where logs and ps show them.
  3. Configure oauth2-proxy (oauth2-proxy.cfg):
http_address = "127.0.0.1:4180"
reverse_proxy = true
trusted_proxy_ips = ["127.0.0.1/32", "::1/128"]
upstreams = ["static://202"]
set_xauthrequest = true

provider = "oidc"
oidc_issuer_url = "https://id.example.org/realms/example"
client_id = "go-slides"
client_secret_file = "/run/secrets/oauth2-proxy-client-secret"
code_challenge_method = "S256"

redirect_url = "/oauth2/callback"
whitelist_domains = ["slides.example.org", "decks.example.org"]
email_domains = ["example.org"]

cookie_secret_file = "/run/secrets/oauth2-proxy-cookie-secret"
cookie_secure = true
cookie_samesite = "lax"

redirect_url without a host brings each site’s sign-in back to its own callback, so each site keeps its own cookie. whitelist_domains is where a sign-in may return to: asked to go anywhere else, it stays on your site. trusted_proxy_ips believes the X-Forwarded-* headers from Caddy alone. email_domains says who may come in; oauth2-proxy also has options for groups and lists of addresses.

  1. Configure Caddy (Caddyfile.oidc):
import headers.caddy

(signed_in) {
 handle /oauth2/* {
 reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:4180
 }
 handle {
 forward_auth 127.0.0.1:4180 {
 uri /oauth2/auth
 copy_headers X-Auth-Request-User X-Auth-Request-Email
 @unauthorized status 401
 handle_response @unauthorized {
 redir * /oauth2/sign_in?rd={scheme}://{hostport}{uri} 302
 }
 }
 {block}
 }
}

slides.example.org {
 import signed_in {
 root * /srv/go-slides-site
 file_server {
 precompressed br gzip
 }
 import playground_headers
 }
}

decks.example.org {
 import signed_in {
 reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080
 }
}
slides -s --allowed-host decks.example.org /srv/decks
oauth2-proxy --config /etc/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy.cfg
caddy run --config Caddyfile.oidc

oauth2-proxy and slides listen on the loopback only: the one way in is through Caddy, and so through the sign-in. The playground’s headers go inside the signed-in block, on the playground alone: oauth2-proxy’s sign-in page is a form, which their form-action 'none' would stop.

The alternative is caddy-security, a Caddy module that does the sign-in inside Caddy, with no second process. It needs a Caddy built with the module (xcaddy), and its own configuration language.

Check it 

curl -sI -H 'Accept-Encoding: br' 'https://slides.example.org/playground/playground.wasm?v=v0.1.0'

The answer says content-type: application/wasm, content-encoding: br and cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable, with the content-security-policy above. With the sign-in in front, the same request without a cookie answers 302 to /oauth2/sign_in.

References

  • Caddy: automatic HTTPS, file_server, header, reverse_proxy, forward_auth.
  • RFC 8555, ACME: HTTP-01 (8.3), DNS-01 (8.4).
  • OpenID Connect Core 1.0: the authorization code flow (3.1), the redirect URI (3.1.2.1), the ID Token (2).
  • oauth2-proxy: configuration, OpenID Connect provider.
